title: JPMorgan Plans 1,000 New Tech Hires in India Even as AI Reshapes Its Workforce
excerpt: The Wall Street giant is doubling down on India's Global Capability Centres for AI, cloud, and cybersecurity talent, even as it deploys artificial intelligence to cut jobs by up to 40% in some business units.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • JPMorgan plans to hire 1,000 tech professionals in India, focusing on AI and cybersecurity.
  • AI has reduced jobs by 30% to 40% in some units, with affected employees redeployed.
  • A new two-million-square-foot campus in Mumbai will support up to 30,000 workers by 2029.
  • India's GCC ecosystem employs 2.36 million people, with AI roles making up 64% of new hiring.

JPMorgan Chase is preparing to hire around 1,000 technology professionals across its Indian operations, expanding its Global Capability Centres in Bengaluru, Mumbai, and Hyderabad at a time when the bank's own leadership acknowledges that artificial intelligence is eliminating roles in other parts of the organisation, according to a report by India Today.

The new positions will focus on high-demand areas including artificial intelligence and machine learning, cloud computing, cybersecurity, advanced data science, and software engineering. The move underscores a deliberate strategy: even as AI automates routine work, JPMorgan is channelling investment into the specialised talent needed to build, deploy, and govern that technology.

AI Cuts Jobs in Some Units, Creates Demand in Others

The expansion arrives against a striking backdrop. During JPMorgan's second-quarter 2026 earnings call, CEO Jamie Dimon said AI had already reduced jobs by 30% to 40% in select units of the bank, with most affected employees offered roles elsewhere in the organisation.

"The whole company's working this at this point."

— Jamie Dimon, CEO, JPMorgan Chase

JPMorgan now has nearly 1,000 AI use cases under development, with about 50 representing the bank's largest efforts across fraud detection, risk management, marketing, and document review. The bank's technology budget has climbed to nearly $20 billion, and its internal AI coding assistant has boosted engineer productivity by 10% to 20%, according to Global Chief Information Officer Lori Beer.

Yet Beer also signalled a shift in hiring philosophy. "We've sort of passed our high growth time," she told Reuters, adding that the bank would "continue to optimise the footprint we have." The India hiring, then, represents a targeted expansion — not a return to the broad-based recruitment drives of previous years, but a focused push for specialists who can build the AI infrastructure the bank is betting its future on.

India's Growing Role in JPMorgan's Global Operations

JPMorgan Chase currently employs more than 50,000 people in India — roughly one-sixth of its global workforce — across technology, operations, and corporate functions. About a third of the bank's 63,000-strong global technology workforce is based in the country, making India its largest technology hub outside the United States.

The bank operates major campuses in all three cities: a 1.16-million-square-foot facility at Nirlon Knowledge Park in Mumbai, a 1.12-million-square-foot hub at Embassy Tech Village in Bengaluru, and offices at the JP Morgan Tower in Hyderabad's HITEC City.

The ambitions go further. JPMorgan is planning a two-million-square-foot campus in Mumbai's Powai district that would be Asia's largest GCC. The facility, expected to be completed by 2029, could support up to 30,000 employees, according to HR Katha. Hiring for this expansion will span software engineering, digital platforms, cybersecurity, data science, finance operations, and corporate functions.

Part of a Broader GCC Surge

India's GCC Growth Surge
›Over 2,100 GCCs in India.
›2.36 million people employed.
›AI roles account for 64% of new hiring.
›Projected 510,000 new jobs by 2026.
Nasscom-Zinnov report

JPMorgan's India hiring fits within a larger trend reshaping the country's technology workforce. India now hosts more than 2,100 Global Capability Centres employing approximately 2.36 million people and generating nearly $100 billion in revenue, according to a 2026 Nasscom-Zinnov report.

The nature of that hiring has shifted dramatically. AI, data science, and automation now drive 64% of new GCC recruitment, up from just 11% in 2021, according to data from foundit, a job postings platform. GCC hiring is projected to reach 510,000 jobs by the end of 2026 — the first time annual recruitment would cross the five-lakh mark.

"Companies are no longer setting up Global Capability Centres simply to reduce costs. They are building them to develop the AI, engineering and product capabilities that run their global businesses."

— Tarun Sinha, CEO, foundit

Other global banks and corporations are making similar moves. Citigroup relocated approximately 1,000 tech jobs to India after cutting its China technology workforce. American Airlines plans to double headcount at its Hyderabad hub to 800, while Southwest Airlines is expanding its GCC to about 1,000 employees.

What This Means for Indian Tech Workers

For India's technology professionals — including those in the diaspora considering a return — JPMorgan's hiring signals a structural shift rather than a cyclical bump. The bank is not simply adding bodies; it is looking for specialists who can work with frontier AI systems, manage cloud-native platforms at enterprise scale, and navigate the regulatory complexity of global financial services.

The competitive dynamics are also worth watching. As Dimon noted, AI tools will become widely available across the industry through technology vendors, meaning the advantage for large banks will come not from having AI, but from having the talent to deploy it effectively. India, with its deep engineering talent pool and established GCC infrastructure, is where much of that competition for talent will play out.

JPMorgan's Q2 2026 results — net income of $16.9 billion, revenue up 15% year over year, and record revenue across every business unit — provide the financial runway to sustain this investment. The question now is whether India's talent pipeline can keep pace with demand that is growing not just in volume but in technical sophistication.
